nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name:  Rachycentron canadum
Common Name: Cobia

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Ostiechthys
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Rachycentridae

Other Common Names:  cabio , sergeantfish (312 327 834), ling, lemonfish (327), black bonito (312), crab-eater (834)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  In the United states, cobia are caught in pound nets, gill nets, and seines (903). Also taken incidentally by shrimp trawlers in the Gulf of Mexico (849).  Smith (834) reported that it was sometimes sold as cero in North Carolina and commercial landings in Chesapeake Bay were reported at 3000 pounds in 1921 (312).  In Florida, 1983 landings were reported as 128,940 pounds worth $82,074 (902).

Recreational:  Cobia is considered to be a favorite game and food fish (327 788) and is caught from boats, beaches, piers, and jetties (849). Reported to be a superb game fish caught trolling, casting, or by baited handline (871).  Baits used for cobia include live fish, squid, cut bait, large shrimp, and artificial spoons (849).  It is said to be especially good smoked (788).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic from Massachusetts to Brazil and Argentina, worldwide in warm waters (788 904).

Within Study Area:  Ranges throughout Florida waters.


Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Cobia are nektonic.  Most often found singly but they are also known to school, especially for spawning (788 849)

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: Cobia move north and west on the gulf coast of Florida in the spring and reported to winter in the Florida Keys (849).  Along the east coast of Florida, cobia exhibit a north-south/spring-fall migration pattern (849)

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body: Habitat Type: Usually found in coastal to open ocean waters (788 871), but smaller individuals are found in saltier bays in the summer (327).  Also found in inlets, bays and among mangroves (871).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: No particular substrate preference has been noted, but cobia often congregate around drifting and floating objects (327).  They are common around sea bouys and other floating shelter (788).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature:  Cobia (size unstated) have been collected from waters of 16.8-32.0 C (849).  Juveniles have been collected in temperatures ranging from 28.0 C (664) to 30 C (603), but larvae have been found in waters with temperatures ranging from 25.9 - 32.0 C (904).

Salinity:  Minimum salinity required by eggs has been stated as 23 ppt (888).  Larvae have been collected in salinities from 27.8 - 37.7 ppt (904).  Juveniles and adults have been reported from freshwater in the Hudson Valley (900) to salinities of 44.5 ppt (603).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual.  Fertilization is by means of externally broadcast sexual products.  There is no evidence of egg guarding.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Smith (834) reported that spawning occurs in summer in Chesapeake Bay, but Hildebrand and Schroeder (312) could not confirm that assertion.  In the Gulf of Mexico, spawning apparently occurs from May or June through September (849).

Fecundity: Fecundity has been reported as 1,935,000 to 5,439,000 eggs per female (901).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body: Larvae/Juveniles/Adults:  Larval development, morphometrics, and pigmentation have been described by Hardy (868).  Cobia apparently grow rapidly and have a moderately long life span (849).  Length-weight relationships and growth equations for cobia from the Chesapeake Bay are also available (849 901).  Females appear to grow faster and attain greater size than males (849).  Maximum size has been variously reported as 84 pounds (312) to 150 pounds (68 kg)(788). maximum length is 1.8 m (6 feet)(788).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Little is known of the diet of larval and young juvenile cobia (849).  The primary diet of adults consists of crustaceans including crabs and shrimp and small fish (312 834).  Squid, small demersal fish such as eels, sea catfish, and sciaenids also form part of the diet (849).
